<div class="page page-article reveal">

  <div class="eyebrow page-eyebrow">Customer Analytics · Case Study</div>
  <h1 class="page-title">Priced for nobody</h1>
  <p class="article-deck">
    The most valuable credit card in the lineup was worth <em>$131</em> a customer —
    nearly triple its nearest rival. It was also the second-worst product the company could have
    launched, because almost nobody would take it.
  </p>

  <dl class="article-meta">
    <div><dt>Role</dt><dd>Analyst</dd></div>
    <div><dt>Case</dt><dd>Credit card product design</dd></div>
    <div><dt>Stack</dt><dd>Python · polars · pyrsm</dd></div>
    <div><dt>Course</dt><dd>MGTA 455, Rady School of Management</dd></div>
  </dl>

  <section class="article-section">
    <h2>The problem</h2>
    <p>A financial-technology company was designing a credit card offer to email to 750,000 prospects.
    Three decisions defined the product:</p>
    <ul>
      <li><strong>APR</strong> — 14.9%, 16.8%, or 19.8%</li>
      <li><strong>Annual fee</strong> — none, or $20</li>
      <li><strong>Rate type</strong> — fixed or variable</li>
    </ul>
    <p>Twelve possible cards. The prospect list splits into three credit-quality segments by bankruptcy
    score — <strong>150</strong>, <strong>200</strong>, and <strong>250</strong>, where higher means
    riskier — at 250,000 people each. Twelve products across three segments makes
    <strong>36 cells</strong>, and the job is to work out which card to send to whom.</p>
    <p>Each email costs <strong>$0.50</strong> in list rental. So for any cell:</p>
    <p><strong>expected profit per email = P(response) × customer lifetime value − $0.50</strong></p>
  </section>

  <section class="article-section">
    <h2>The tension in one line</h2>
    <p>Every lever that makes a card more valuable makes it less attractive.</p>
    <p>Raise the APR and each customer earns more interest — but fewer sign up. Add a $20 annual fee
    and lifetime value rises by roughly $31 — but response collapses. The two effects pull in opposite
    directions, and profit is their product, so neither one on its own tells you anything.</p>
    <p>Build a card below and watch both numbers move.</p>
  </section>

  <div class="article-panel">
    <div class="article-panel-title">Design a card</div>
    <div class="article-panel-sub">All figures come from a logistic response model fitted to the round-one
    test, combined with the case's lifetime-value estimates for each product and segment.</div>
    <div class="article-design">
      <div>
        <div class="article-ctrl">
          <div class="article-ctrl-lab">Annual percentage rate</div>
          <div class="article-opts" id="c-apr"></div>

          <div class="article-ctrl-lab">Annual fee</div>
          <div class="article-opts" id="c-fee"></div>
        </div>
        <div class="article-ctrl">
          <div class="article-ctrl-lab">Rate type</div>
          <div class="article-opts" id="c-type"></div>
        </div>
        <div class="article-ctrl">
          <div class="article-ctrl-lab">Send to segment</div>
          <div class="article-opts" id="c-bk"></div>
        </div>
      </div>
      <div>
        <div class="article-cardface">
          <div class="article-cf-top" id="cf-seg">Bankruptcy score 150</div>
          <div>
            <div class="article-cf-apr" id="cf-apr">14.9%</div>
            <div class="article-cf-terms" id="cf-terms">Fixed rate · No annual fee</div>

      </div>
    </div>
  </div>

  <section class="article-section">
    <div class="article-callout">
      <p>Try the 19.8% fixed card with a $20 fee on segment 150. It carries the highest lifetime value
      in the entire grid — <strong>$131</strong> — and returns <strong>9 cents</strong> an email,
      because only 0.45% of people accept it. Then drop the fee: value falls to $100, response rises
      more than threefold, and profit jumps to <strong>$1.00</strong>.</p>
    </div>
  </section>

  <section class="article-section">
    <h2>All thirty-six cells at once</h2>
    <p>Laid out together, the structure is obvious in a way it never was in a spreadsheet.</p>
  </section>

  <div class="article-panel">
    <div class="article-panel-title">Expected profit per email</div>
    <div class="article-panel-sub">Twelve products down, three credit segments across. Red cells lose money.
    Hover for the underlying response rate and lifetime value.</div>
    <div class="article-chart-host">
      <div class="article-hm-scroll" id="heat"></div>
      <div class="article-tip" id="tip"></div>
    </div>
    <div class="article-hm-key">
      <span>Loses money</span>
      <div class="article-hm-ramp">
        <span style="background:var(--neg-2)"></span><span style="background:var(--neg-1)"></span>
        <span style="background:var(--mid)"></span><span style="background:var(--pos-1)"></span>
        <span style="background:var(--pos-2)"></span><span style="background:var(--pos-3)"></span>
        <span style="background:var(--pos-4)"></span>
      </div>
      <span>$2.33 per email</span>
    </div>
  </div>

  <section class="article-section">
    <p>Three things fall out immediately.</p>
    <p><strong>Every no-fee card beats every fee-bearing card at the same APR.</strong> Without
    exception, across all three segments. The $20 fee is never worth what it costs in response.</p>
    <p><strong>The riskiest segment is worth far less.</strong> The 250 column is pale throughout —
    its best cell earns $0.68 against $2.33 for the safest segment, because lifetime values there are
    $30 lower on every product.</p>
    <p><strong>Two cells actually lose money.</strong> The 14.9% fixed no-fee card — the single most
    profitable product for the safest segment — is the <em>worst</em> choice for the riskiest one,
    at <strong>−$0.36</strong> an email. Its lifetime value in that segment is $2, which cannot cover a
    50-cent stamp at any response rate.</p>

    <div class="article-callout">
      <p>That reversal is the case in miniature. The same product swings from best to worst depending
      on who receives it. A single company-wide "best card" doesn't exist.</p>
    </div>
  </section>

  <section class="article-section">
    <h2>What I recommended</h2>
    <p>Round one tests three candidate offers per segment on 12,000 prospects. Round two sends the
    winner to the remaining 238,000 in each segment:</p>
  </section>

  <div class="article-tbl-wrap">
    <table class="article-table">
      <thead><tr><th>Segment</th><th>Card</th><th>Per email</th><th>Emails</th><th>Expected profit</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody>
        <tr><td>BK 150</td><td>14.9% fixed, no fee</td><td>$2.3276</td><td>238,000</td><td>$553,971</td></tr>
        <tr><td>BK 200</td><td>14.9% variable, no fee</td><td>$1.6990</td><td>238,000</td><td>$404,357</td></tr>
        <tr><td>BK 250</td><td>16.8% variable, no fee</td><td>$0.6821</td><td>238,000</td><td>$162,341</td></tr>
      </tbody>
      <tfoot><tr><td>Round two total</td><td></td><td></td><td>714,000</td><td>$1,120,669</td></tr></tfoot>
    </table>
  </div>

  <section class="article-section">
    <p>Three segments, three different cards — and notice they differ in <em>every</em> attribute
    except the absent annual fee. The safest segment gets the lowest rate, fixed. The middle segment
    gets the same rate but variable. The riskiest gets a higher rate, variable — because at 14.9% the
    economics in that segment simply don't work.</p>
  </section>

  <div class="article-stats">
    <div class="article-stat"><div class="article-stat-v">$1.12M</div><div class="article-stat-l">Expected round-two profit</div></div>
    <div class="article-stat"><div class="article-stat-v">3.4×</div><div class="article-stat-l">Best segment vs worst, per email</div></div>
    <div class="article-stat"><div class="article-stat-v">0</div><div class="article-stat-l">Segments where the fee wins</div></div>
    <div class="article-stat"><div class="article-stat-v">$2.68</div><div class="article-stat-l">Spread between best and worst cell</div></div>
  </div>

  <section class="article-section">
    <h2>The technical layer</h2>
    <div class="article-tech-label">For readers who want the mechanics</div>

    <details class="article-details">
    <summary>Predicting cells that were never tested</summary>
    <div class="article-det-body">
    <p>The round-one test did not run all 36 combinations — it ran a subset. Filling in the rest means
    fitting a logistic model on the tested cells, with APR, annual fee, rate type and bankruptcy score as
    predictors, and using it to predict the untested ones.</p>
    <p>This is the load-bearing assumption of the whole analysis. The model treats each attribute as
    contributing independently to the log odds of response, so a prediction for an untested combination
    is an extrapolation from cells that share its individual features, not an observation.</p>
    <p>If real customers respond to <em>combinations</em> — say a variable rate is tolerable at 14.9%
    but alarming at 19.8% — an additive model cannot see that, and its predictions for untested corners
    will be confidently wrong. Adding interaction terms would test this, and with only a handful of
    tested cells there is not much room to fit them.</p>
    </div>
    </details>

    <details class="article-details">
    <summary>Why lifetime value moves with the product</summary>
    <div class="article-det-body">
    <p>Lifetime value isn't a property of the customer alone — it's a property of the customer holding a
    particular card. A higher APR earns more interest per dollar of balance, so value rises with rate. An
    annual fee adds roughly $20 of revenue and about $31 of modelled value. And riskier segments carry
    about $30 less value on every product, reflecting expected losses.</p>
    <p>The extreme case is the 14.9% fixed no-fee card in segment 250, valued at <strong>$2</strong>. At
    that level no response rate can save it: even universal acceptance yields $2 against a $0.50 cost per
    email sent to everyone, and at the modelled 7.2% response the cell loses money.</p>
    </div>
    </details>

    <details class="article-details">
    <summary>What the round-one budget actually buys</summary>
    <div class="article-det-body">
    <p>Testing three offers on 12,000 prospects per segment means 4,000 emails per offer. At response
    rates between 0.5% and 7%, that yields somewhere between 20 and 280 responses per cell.</p>
    <p>The low end is the problem. Twenty responses gives a standard error large enough that two offers
    a percentage point apart are indistinguishable. The test is well powered for the strong offers and
    underpowered for the weak ones — which is tolerable, since the purpose is to identify a winner rather
    than to estimate every cell precisely.</p>
    <p>The reported $1.12M also excludes the cost of round one itself — 36,000 emails at $0.50, or
    $18,000 — and counts only round-two profit.</p>
    </div>
    </details>

    <details class="article-details">
    <summary>What I'd do differently</summary>
    <div class="article-det-body">
    <p><strong>Put uncertainty on the recommendation.</strong> For segment 150 the top two offers sit at
    $2.3276 and $2.3145 per email — a gap of 1.3 cents. Scaled to 238,000 emails that's $3,100, well
    inside what sampling error can produce. I named a winner where the honest answer is a tie, and the
    tie is worth knowing because the two cards differ in rate type.</p>
    <p><strong>Test the additivity assumption.</strong> Fit the model with and without interaction terms
    and compare on held-out cells. If predictions barely move, the extrapolation is trustworthy; if they
    move a lot, the untested corners of the grid need actual testing.</p>
    <p><strong>Reconsider what round one is for.</strong> Spending it on the three offers the model
    already likes confirms what the model believes. Spending it on the cells where the model is
    <em>least certain</em> would buy more information — a design question rather than a modelling one.</p>
    <p><strong>Sanity-check the fee result.</strong> That no fee-bearing card wins in any segment is a
    clean finding, but it rests on a modelled $31 value increment against a modelled response penalty.
    Both come from the same limited test, and a result that uniform deserves a second look before a
    company builds a product line on it.</p>
    </div>
    </details>
  </section>

  <section class="article-section">
    <h2>What this case taught me</h2>
    <p><strong>Per-customer value and total profit are different objectives, and optimising the first can
    destroy the second.</strong> The highest-value card in the grid returns nine cents an email. Value
    per acquisition means nothing until you multiply it by how many people accept — and the levers that
    raise one systematically lower the other.</p>
    <p><strong>"Best" is a question about a pairing, not a product.</strong> The card that earns $2.33 in
    the safest segment loses 36 cents in the riskiest. Any recommendation phrased as a single best
    product is answering a question nobody asked.</p>
    <p><strong>And a grid of 36 numbers is a better analyst than a model summary.</strong> The most useful
    artefact here wasn't a coefficient table — it was the cell-by-cell profit map, where the pattern in
    the annual-fee column was visible instantly and needed no statistics to defend.</p>
    <div class="chips article-chips">
      <span class="chip">Product design analytics</span>
      <span class="chip">Logistic regression</span>
      <span class="chip">Design of experiments</span>
      <span class="chip">Segment-level targeting</span>
      <span class="chip">CLV modeling</span>
      <span class="chip">Profit optimization</span>
      <span class="chip">polars</span>
    </div>
    <p class="article-fine">Figures are from my own analysis on the course dataset. The underlying case materials
    and data are proprietary to the publisher and are not reproduced here.</p>
  </section>
</div>

  (function(){
    var COST=0.50, SEG=250000;
    var O=[
     {o:1, apr:14.9,t:"Fixed",   f:20, r:[.016694,.019343,.022403], c:[83,63,33]},
     {o:2, apr:14.9,t:"Variable",f:20, r:[.013845,.016049,.018599], c:[93,73,43]},

     {o:4, apr:14.9,t:"Variable",f:0,  r:[.045395,.052357,.060319], c:[62,42,12]},
     {o:5, apr:16.8,t:"Fixed",   f:20, r:[.010043,.011649,.013509], c:[103,83,53]},
     {o:6, apr:16.8,t:"Variable",f:20, r:[.008319,.009653,.011198], c:[113,93,63]},
     {o:7, apr:16.8,t:"Fixed",   f:0,  r:[.033221,.038390,.044328], c:[72,52,22]},
     {o:8, apr:16.8,t:"Variable",f:0,  r:[.027631,.031960,.036941], c:[82,62,32]},
     {o:9, apr:19.8,t:"Fixed",   f:20, r:[.004479,.005200,.006037], c:[131,111,81]},
     {o:10,apr:19.8,t:"Variable",f:20, r:[.003707,.004304,.004998], c:[141,121,91]},
     {o:11,apr:19.8,t:"Fixed",   f:0,  r:[.015012,.017399,.020158], c:[100,80,50]},
     {o:12,apr:19.8,t:"Variable",f:0,  r:[.012446,.014432,.016728], c:[110,90,60]}
    ];
    var BK=[150,200,250];
    function prof(o,i){return o.r[i]*o.c[i]-COST;}
    function usd(v){return (v<0?"−$":"$")+Math.abs(v).toFixed(2);}
    function usd0(v){return (v<0?"−$":"$")+Math.abs(Math.round(v)).toLocaleString("en-US");}

    var sel={apr:14.9,fee:0,type:"Fixed",bk:0};
    function opts(host,vals,labels,key){
      host.innerHTML="";
      vals.forEach(function(v,i){
        var b=document.createElement("button");
        b.className="opt"; b.type="button"; b.textContent=labels[i];
        b.setAttribute("aria-pressed", sel[key]===v);
        b.addEventListener("click",function(){sel[key]=v;renderAll();});
        host.appendChild(b);
      });
    }
    function current(){
      for(var i=0;i<O.length;i++){
        if(O[i].apr===sel.apr && O[i].f===sel.fee && O[i].t===sel.type) return O[i];
      }
      return O[0];
    }
    function renderAll(){
      opts(document.getElementById("c-apr"),[14.9,16.8,19.8],["14.9%","16.8%","19.8%"],"apr");
      opts(document.getElementById("c-fee"),[0,20],["No fee","$20 / year"],"fee");
      opts(document.getElementById("c-type"),["Fixed","Variable"],["Fixed rate","Variable rate"],"type");
      opts(document.getElementById("c-bk"),[0,1,2],["BK 150","BK 200","BK 250"],"bk");
      var o=current(), i=sel.bk, r=o.r[i], c=o.c[i], p=prof(o,i);
      document.getElementById("cf-apr").textContent=o.apr.toFixed(1)+"%";
      document.getElementById("cf-terms").textContent=
        o.t+" rate · "+(o.f===0?"No annual fee":"$20 annual fee");
      document.getElementById("cf-seg").textContent="Bankruptcy score "+BK[i];
      document.getElementById("ledger").innerHTML=
        "<div class='led-row'><span class='led-k'>Predicted response</span><span class='led-v'>"+
          (r*100).toFixed(2)+"%</span></div>"+
        "<div class='led-row'><span class='led-k'>Lifetime value if they accept</span><span class='led-v'>$"+
          c+"</span></div>"+
        "<div class='led-row'><span class='led-k'>Expected value per email</span><span class='led-v'>"+
          usd(r*c)+"</span></div>"+
        "<div class='led-row'><span class='led-k'>− list rental</span><span class='led-v'>−$0.50</span></div>"+
        "<div class='led-row tot'><span>Profit per email</span><span class='led-v'>"+usd(p)+"</span></div>"+
        "<div class='led-row'><span class='led-k'>× 250,000 in segment</span><span class='led-v'>"+
          usd0(p*SEG)+"</span></div>";
      var ranked=O.map(function(x){return {o:x,p:prof(x,i)};})
                  .sort(function(a,b){return b.p-a.p;});
      var pos=ranked.findIndex(function(x){return x.o.o===o.o;})+1;
      var best=ranked[0];
      document.getElementById("rank").innerHTML= pos===1
        ? "<strong>Best of 12</strong> for this segment. Nothing else in the lineup earns more here."
        : "Ranks <strong>"+pos+" of 12</strong> for this segment. The winner is "+
          best.o.apr.toFixed(1)+"% "+best.o.t.toLowerCase()+
          (best.o.f===0?", no fee":", $20 fee")+" at <strong>"+usd(best.p)+
          "</strong> per email — "+usd(best.p-prof(o,i))+" more.";
    }
    renderAll();

    (function(){
      var t=document.getElementById("heat"), tip=document.getElementById("tip"),
          host=t.parentNode;
      var vals=[]; O.forEach(function(o){BK.forEach(function(_,i){vals.push(prof(o,i));});});
      var max=Math.max.apply(null,vals), min=Math.min.apply(null,vals);
      function shade(v){
        if(v<0) return v<min/2 ? "var(--neg-2)" : "var(--neg-1)";
        var f=v/max;
        if(f<0.14) return "var(--mid)";
        if(f<0.30) return "var(--pos-1)";
        if(f<0.52) return "var(--pos-2)";
        if(f<0.78) return "var(--pos-3)";
        return "var(--pos-4)";
      }
      function ink(v){
        if(v<0) return v<min/2 ? "#fff" : "var(--ink)";
        var f=v/max;
        return f>=0.52 ? "#fff" : "var(--ink)";
      }
      var html="<thead><tr><th class='rowh'>Card</th>";
      BK.forEach(function(b){html+="<th>BK "+b+"</th>";});
      html+="</tr></thead><tbody>";
      O.forEach(function(o){
        html+="<tr><th class='rowh'>"+o.apr.toFixed(1)+"% "+o.t.toLowerCase()+
              (o.f===0?", no fee":", $20 fee")+"</th>";
        BK.forEach(function(b,i){
          var p=prof(o,i);
          html+="<td><div class='cell' data-o='"+o.o+"' data-i='"+i+"' style='background:"+
                shade(p)+";color:"+ink(p)+"'>"+usd(p)+"</div></td>";
        });
        html+="</tr>";
      });
      var tbl=document.createElement("table");
      tbl.className="hm";
      tbl.innerHTML=html+"</tbody>";
      t.appendChild(tbl);
      t.querySelectorAll(".cell").forEach(function(c){
        c.addEventListener("mouseenter",function(){
          var o=O[+c.dataset.o-1], i=+c.dataset.i, p=prof(o,i);
          tip.innerHTML="<b>"+o.apr.toFixed(1)+"% "+o.t.toLowerCase()+
            (o.f===0?", no fee":", $20 fee")+" · BK "+BK[i]+"</b><br>"+
            (o.r[i]*100).toFixed(2)+"% respond · $"+o.c[i]+" lifetime value<br>"+
            usd(p)+" per email · "+usd0(p*SEG)+" per segment";
          tip.style.opacity=1;
          var hb=host.getBoundingClientRect(),bb=c.getBoundingClientRect();
          var lx=bb.left-hb.left+bb.width/2-tip.offsetWidth/2;
          tip.style.left=Math.max(4,Math.min(lx,hb.width-tip.offsetWidth-4))+"px";
          tip.style.top=(bb.top-hb.top-tip.offsetHeight-8)+"px";
        });
        c.addEventListener("mouseleave",function(){tip.style.opacity=0;});
      });
    })();
  })();
</script>
